title: The Platform Sutra
hookLine: the teachings of Huineng, the sixth patriarch, as his students remembered them
last: NOT TWO, AND NOT CLINGING TO ONE.

cards: A young man is selling firewood in a market town in the far south of China. He's poor. The sutra says his father died when he was small, and he and his mother live on what the wood brings in.
He delivers a bundle to a customer's lodging, and on his way out he hears a man inside reciting a sutra, the Diamond Sutra. He stops. Something in him opens at the words.
He asks where the man learned it: a monastery to the north, where a teacher named Hongren teaches. The young man's name is Huineng.

teach.b: The Platform Sutra presents itself as Huineng's own talks, given from a teaching seat, a raised platform, at a temple, and written down by his students. It opens with him telling his life, starting with the firewood.

Huineng arrives at Hongren's monastery and asks to become a Buddha. Hongren tests him: you're from the south, a barbarian, he says, using a rough word for southern people. How could you become a Buddha?

teach.h: NO NORTH OR SOUTH IN BUDDHA-NATURE.
teach.b: Huineng answers: people may be northern or southern, but Buddha-nature has no north or south. Hongren says nothing more for the moment and sends him to the back to split wood and pound rice.
Then, two verses on a wall. Hongren asks his monks to write a verse showing what they've understood.
The senior monk, Shenxiu, writes, in paraphrase: the body is the tree of awakening, the mind a bright mirror on its stand; wipe it again and again, and let no dust settle.
Huineng can't read or write, the sutra says, so he asks someone to put his verse up beside it.
In one widely retold version: awakening has no tree, the mirror has no stand; from the beginning there is not one thing, so where would dust settle?
Hongren calls him in secret, teaches him at night, and names him his heir, and so tradition calls Huineng the sixth patriarch.
The rest of the Platform Sutra is his teaching, and the coming days are spent inside it.

how: In Zen and Chan communities the Platform Sutra is studied, and the story of Huineng's arrival and the two verses on the wall is retold in talks.

o: a sermon the Buddha gave from a raised stage
a set of rules for building temple altars
Huineng's talks, given from a teaching seat

games.q: the Platform Sutra: tap the pairs.
p: the teacher who named him heir

s: Huineng wrote his verse on the wall with his own hand
the sutra says he couldn't read or write, and asked someone to put it up for him.
the sutra opens with Huineng telling his own life story
it begins with the firewood, the market and the Diamond Sutra through a doorway.
Hongren welcomed Huineng with open arms at their first meeting
he tested him, calling him a southern barbarian and asking how he could become a Buddha.

games.q: you've walked a long way to a well-known teacher. he looks at you and says: you're a southerner, a barbarian. how could you become a Buddha? what do you say?
o: people have north and south; Buddha-nature doesn't
games.why: that was Huineng's answer. Hongren said nothing more for the moment and sent him to pound rice, but he had heard it.

practice: Huineng's story begins with the plainest line he could give: a poor boy, a widowed mother, a load of firewood.

Let the first plain line of your own story come up, the way you'd tell it if you weren't trying to impress anyone, and hear it once without polishing it. Then let it go, and rest in the breath, carrying no bundle at all.

wordCard.voice: The Platform Sutra. The teachings of Huineng, told from a teaching seat and remembered by his students, opening with his own story. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (Liuzu Tanjing): 'the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch'.

carryVoice: Your line: the sixth patriarch. A woodcutter from the south, and a Buddha-nature with no north or south. Rest well.
